ad11_who_pays.topic: Who pays: federal, state and local tax distribution; payroll cap; capital gains; Saez-Zucman dispute; 2025 law distribution

claims.text: CBO (Sept 2026, 2023 data): average federal tax rates fell for every income group 1979-2023, most for the lowest quintile; individual income tax rates 2023 ranged from -11% (lowest quintile) to 16% (highest); top quintile paid 70% of federal taxes (55% in 1979), top 1% paid 26% (14% in 1979); top 1% share of income after transfers and taxes 7% (1979) to 13% (2023).

Tax Foundation reading of CBO 2022 data: average federal tax rate (all federal taxes) lowest quintile 1.4%, highest quintile 23.2%, top 1% 31.5%; payroll tax rate bottom 20% 9.5% vs top 20% 6.1%; individual income tax bottom -10.1%, top 16.6%; lowest quintile federal rate -16.5% (2020), -22.5% (2021); top 1% share of federal taxes 14.1% (1979) to 27.3% (2022); bottom 80% share of federal taxes 44.8% (1979) to 29.6% (2022) while its income share fell 54.6% to 45.1%.

CBO total effective federal tax rates by quintile (older CBO method, comprehensive household income): 1979 lowest 8.0, second 14.3, middle 18.6, fourth 21.2, highest 27.5, top 1% 37.0; 2000 lowest 6.4, middle 16.6, highest 28.0, top1 33.0; 2007 lowest 4.0, middle 14.3, highest 25.1, top1 29.5.

ITEP Who Pays 7th ed. (2024 law, 2023 incomes): US average state and local taxes as share of family income: lowest 20% 11.3%, second 10.4%, middle 10.5%, fourth 10.3%, next 15% 9.5%, next 4% 8.3%, top 1% 7.2%; lowest 20% pay 7% in sales/excise, 4.4% property, -0.2% income; top 1% 1%, 1.9%, 4.1%.

ITEP 2024 (all federal, state and local taxes): total effective rates lowest 20% 17.1%, second 22.2%, middle 26.4%, fourth 27.2%, next 15% 28.8%, next 4% 30.1%, top 1% 34.8%, all 29.2%; top 1% receives 20.1% of income and pays 23.9% of all taxes; lowest 20% receives 2.6% and pays 1.5%. ITEP calls the system 'just barely progressive'.

Saez and Zucman estimated the richest 400 families paid 23% of income in all taxes in 2018 vs 24.2% for the bottom half; TPC (Gleckman) criticised exclusion of refundable credits, extrapolation from older data, small sample; TPC estimated federal rates 2.9% bottom 20%, 30.6% top 0.1%.

Balkir, Saez, Yagan, Zucman (2025): wealthiest ~400 paid about 24% of economic income 2018-2020 vs ~30% for the population; Splinter's adjustments give 38% for the top group and 25% for the population; Cato's Michel cites ranges 38-73% including giving.
Social Security tax: 6.2% employee + 6.2% employer on earnings up to $184,500 in 2026 ($176,100 in 2025); Medicare 1.45% each on all earnings; self-employed 15.3%.
2025 long-term capital gains rates: 0%, 15% from $48,350 (single), 20% above $533,400 single / $600,050 married joint; 3.8% net investment income tax can bring top rate to 23.8%.

CBO on Public Law 119-21 (2025 reconciliation law), 2026-2034: resources decrease for households toward the bottom and increase for the middle and top; excludes debt service and macro effects; in-kind transfers down $900bn mainly Medicaid and SNAP.
Reported CBO decile figures (Aug 2025): lowest decile loses about $1,200 a year on average (3.1% of income); fifth and sixth deciles gain $800-$1,200; top decile gains about $13,600 a year.

2026 EITC two children: earned income amount $18,290, maximum $7,316, phase-out begins $23,890 ($31,160 MFJ), ends $58,629 ($65,899 MFJ); CTC $2,200 per child, $1,700 refundable; standard deduction HoH $24,150.

Kenan Tax Center: 2014 IRS top-400 returns reported about $5.68bn salaries and wages, $5.39bn interest, $13.84bn dividends and $76.84bn capital asset sales; results depend on whether EITC, state, payroll and corporate taxes are counted; credits Splinter, with Gerald Auten, for testing all reasonable design choices.
CBO (Sept 2026): transfers and federal taxes reduced income inequality in every year 1979-2023, and the reduction was larger in 2023 than in most years since 1979.

ad11_fees.topic: Fees everywhere: FTC junk-fee rule, utility shutoffs, fines and fees as local revenue (Ferguson), licence suspensions

claims.text: FTC rule on unfair or deceptive fees: announced 17 Dec 2024 (vote 4-1, Commissioner Andrew Ferguson dissenting), effective 12 May 2025; covers live-event tickets (incl. resale) and short-term lodging; requires total price up front; does not ban any type or amount of fee; FTC projected up to 53 million hours a year of consumer time saved, valued at over $11bn over ten years.
Taxes, shipping and optional add-ons may be excluded from the advertised total but must be disclosed before payment; civil penalties up to $51,744 per violation.

EIA 2024 Residential Utility Disconnections Report (Apr 2026): 15.1m residential shutoffs in 2024 (13.4m electric, 1.7m gas); 122m final disconnection notices; 12.6m reconnections; survey covers 93.5% of electric and 96.1% of gas customers; first comprehensive federal collection.

DOJ Ferguson report (4 Mar 2015): fines and fees $1.38m of $11.07m general fund revenue FY2010; $2.46m collected FY2013; $3.09m budgeted of $13.26m FY2015; over 9,000 warrants issued in 2013; 'focus on revenue rather than by public safety needs'; officials' emails on raising ticket revenue.

Governing (2019): nearly 600 jurisdictions drew more than 10% of general fund revenue from fines and forfeitures, at least 284 over 20%; Georgetown, La. 92%; median among 50 largest cities 2%; most local governments under 5%; figures are low estimates.

NCSL (2024): since 2017 at least 25 states and DC curbed or ended debt-based licence suspensions; nearly 11 million people have faced such suspensions (Michigan law review estimate); NJ study: nearly 45% of suspended drivers lost jobs; Brennan Center 2019: more than 42 cents spent per dollar collected; California on-time collection rose 8.9% after ending suspensions.

FTC announced 9 April 2026 a $10m settlement (consumer redress) with the largest US ticket-resale platform (filings reference StubHub) under the FTC Act and the Fees Rule, alleging failure to show all-in prices at all stages and deliberate delay in compliance; no admission.

ad11_cliff.topic: Benefits cliff: Atlanta Fed CLIFF, ASPE EMTRs, CBO EMTR, SNAP, Medicaid, ACA subsidy cliff, CCDF, EITC counter-evidence

claims.text: Atlanta Fed defines a benefits cliff as career advancement leaving a family financially worse off through partial or complete loss of benefits; loss of benefits as income rises acts like an effective marginal tax. Worked example 'Leia', single mother of two in Clarke County, Georgia: concessions worker to CNA path shows a decline of more than $11,000 in net resources over the first three years; CNA to LPN a loss exceeding $35,000 over the first three years; both positive over a lifetime.

Atlanta Fed (Aug 2026): CCDF childcare eligibility ends at 85% of state median income, a steep cliff in many states; state responses include Florida School Readiness Plus phase-out to 100% SMI, Indiana disregard of up to $15,000 of increased earnings for TANF, Maine 100% earned-income disregard for three months, Colorado and Massachusetts eliminating TANF asset limits, Ohio Benefits Bridge up to $8,000, Tennessee Our Chance TN.
Atlanta Fed cites a 2021 Florida Chamber Foundation survey: about one in three businesses reported employees or candidates declining jobs, hours or advancement for fear of losing benefits.

ASPE 2019 (TRIM3, 2014 data): CCDF households at 100-149% of poverty face median MTR 67% on a $2,000 raise, 73% on $5,000 (net gain $1,350), 79% on $10,000 (net $2,100); after a $2,000 raise 10% of CCDF households face a cliff (MTR >= 100%), 15% negative MTR; at 100-199% of poverty a $10,000 raise causes 37% to lose the entire subsidy (median loss $4,400).

CBO: workers below 450% of poverty guidelines face an average effective marginal tax rate of 31% in 2016 (income and payroll taxes, SNAP phase-out, ACA subsidies); rates vary greatly, especially at low earnings.

Kleven (2024): 'a strong consensus posits' sizable EITC employment effects; apart from the 1993 federal reform, EITC expansions show no clear robust employment effects; ~500 event-study estimates centred on zero.

ACA subsidy cliff returned in 2026 after enhanced credits expired: cutoff $84,600 for a household of two (400% of 2025 FPL); Charleston WV 63-year-old couple at $85,000: lowest-cost Bronze from $0 (2025) to $3,648/month (2026); at $84,500 benchmark silver capped a little under 10% of income (~$700/month).

H.R. 1 SNAP: work requirement extended to ages 18-64 and parent exemption limited to children under 14 (on enactment, 4 July 2025); state share of administrative costs to 75% from 1 Oct 2026; states pay 0-15% of benefits by error rate from FY2028; Thrifty Food Plan re-evaluations cost-neutral.
SNAP FY2027 (48 states and DC): gross monthly limit (130% of poverty) $1,729 for one, $2,960 for three; net limit $1,330 / $2,277; maximum allotment $306 / $808.
SNAP benefit formula assumes households spend 30% of net income on food; gross income generally below 130% FPL, net below 100%.
